items.why: Adrenal glands sit superior to the kidneys; make aldosterone, sex hormones, corticosteroids

questions.q: Which hormone is produced by the gland that sits on the superior pole of the kidney?
questions.explain: The adrenal (suprarenal) glands sit above the kidneys and make aldosterone, sex hormones, and corticosteroids.

items.why: Psoas: posterior to lower kidney; ureters descend on its anterior surface

questions.q: As the ureter descends from the renal hilum, it runs along the anterior surface of which muscle?
questions.explain: The ureters begin at the hilum and descend anterior to the psoas muscles before crossing the common iliac vessels.

items.why: Quadratus lumborum: lateral, posterior to the lower kidney

questions.q: Which muscle lies immediately posterior to the lower kidney, lateral to the psoas?
questions.explain: The medial psoas and the lateral quadratus lumborum lie immediately posterior to the lower parts of the kidneys.

items.why: Renal capsule: fibrous outer layer; surrounded by perinephric fat then renal fascia

questions.q: What tissue makes up the renal capsule?
questions.explain: The renal capsule is fibrous connective tissue that gives the kidney a smooth, firm surface.

questions.q: Moving outward, which layer lies immediately outside the renal capsule?
questions.explain: The capsule is surrounded by perinephric (perirenal) fat, which is covered by the renal (perinephric) fascia.

items.why: Cortex: renal corpuscles + convoluted tubules; primary filtration site

questions.q: Which structures are found in the renal cortex?
choices: Loops of Henle and collecting ducts
questions.explain: The cortex lies beneath the capsule and contains renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules.

questions.q: The renal cortex is the primary site of which process?
questions.explain: Containing the renal corpuscles, the cortex is the primary site of blood filtration and early urine modification.

items.why: Medulla: inner region made of renal pyramids

questions.q: The renal medulla is composed mainly of which structures?
questions.explain: The renal medulla is composed of cone-shaped renal pyramids.

items.why: Pyramids: loops of Henle + collecting ducts; urine concentration

questions.q: The loops of Henle and collecting ducts in the renal pyramids are critical for what?
questions.explain: Renal pyramids contain loops of Henle and collecting ducts, which are critical for urine concentration.

items.why: Renal columns: cortical extensions between pyramids; vessel pathways

questions.q: What is the main role of the renal columns?
choices: Carry vessels between cortex and medulla
Drain urine from papillae to calyces
Anchor the kidney to renal fascia
questions.explain: Renal columns are cortical extensions between pyramids that serve as pathways for blood vessels traveling between cortex and medulla.

items.why: Papillae drain urine from pyramids into minor calyces

questions.q: Urine leaving the renal papillae drains first into which structure?
questions.explain: Urine formed in the pyramids drains from the renal papillae into minor calyces.

items.why: Minor calyces merge into major calyces

questions.q: Minor calyces merge to form which structures?
questions.explain: Minor calyces merge to form major calyces, which funnel urine into the renal pelvis.

items.why: Major calyces funnel urine into the renal pelvis

questions.q: Major calyces funnel urine directly into which structure?
questions.explain: Major calyces funnel urine into the renal pelvis and then the ureter.

items.why: Renal pelvis -> ureter at the UPJ (stone site)

questions.q: Where the renal pelvis narrows into the ureter is a common site for what?
questions.explain: The ureteropelvic junction is one of three common ureteral narrowings where kidney stones get stuck.

items.why: Hilum: medial gateway for renal artery, vein, pelvis/ureter, lymphatics

questions.q: On which aspect of the kidney is the renal hilum located?
questions.explain: The renal hilum is a medial indentation where the renal pelvis, artery, vein, and ureter enter or exit.

questions.q: Lymphatics leaving the left kidney at the hilum drain primarily to which nodes?
questions.explain: All renal lymphatics exit at the hilum; the left kidney drains primarily to para-aortic (lumbar) nodes.

items.why: Ureters: 25-30 cm; three narrowings (UPJ, pelvic brim, UVJ); pass under uterine a.

questions.q: Approximately how long is each ureter?
questions.explain: The ureters are smooth muscle-lined tubes about 25-30 cm long connecting the kidneys to the bladder.

questions.q: Besides the UPJ and UVJ, where else do kidney stones commonly lodge in the ureter?
choices: Iliac vessel crossing at the brim
questions.explain: The three common narrowings are the ureteropelvic junction, the pelvic brim where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels, and the ureterovesical junction.

questions.q: In females, the pelvic segment of the ureter passes inferior to which artery?
questions.explain: In females, the pelvic ureter crosses inferior to the uterine artery.

items.why: Apex: anterior, directed toward the pubic symphysis

questions.q: The apex of the bladder points toward which structure?
questions.explain: The bladder apex is anterior, directed toward the pubic symphysis.

items.why: Body: main expandable portion; superior bladder lymph to external iliac nodes

questions.q: Lymph from the superior part of the bladder drains to which nodes?
questions.explain: Superior bladder lymphatics drain to external iliac nodes; inferior bladder lymphatics drain to internal iliac nodes.

items.why: Fundus: posterior base where the ureters enter

questions.q: Which structures enter the bladder at its fundus (base)?
questions.explain: The fundus is the posterior base of the bladder where the ureters enter.

items.why: Neck: inferior, narrows into the urethra; inferior bladder lymph to internal iliac

questions.q: The bladder neck narrows inferiorly into which structure?
questions.explain: The neck is the inferior region of the bladder that narrows into the urethra.

questions.q: Lymph from the inferior bladder drains to which nodes?
questions.explain: Lymphatic vessels from the inferior bladder drain into the internal iliac nodes.

items.why: Ureteric orifices: oblique entry, no valve, compression prevents reflux

questions.q: What prevents reflux of urine into the ureters during voiding?
choices: Oblique passage through the bladder wall
A discrete flap valve at each orifice
questions.explain: The ureters pass obliquely through the bladder musculature without a discrete valve, so bladder contraction compresses the orifices and prevents reflux.

items.why: Trigone: smooth triangle of ureteric orifices + internal urethral orifice; stretch sensation

questions.q: Which three openings define the trigone?
choices: Both ureteric orifices and external urethral orifice
One ureteric orifice and both urethral orifices
Both ureteric orifices and internal urethral orifice
Both ureteric orifices and the urachal opening
questions.explain: The trigone is a smooth triangular region on the posterior wall defined by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice.

questions.q: Stretch sensed in the region of the trigone triggers contraction of which muscle?
questions.explain: Sensory fibers stimulated by stretch, particularly in the trigone, lead the detrusor to contract and empty the bladder.

items.why: Internal urethral orifice: opening of the bladder into the urethra (trigone apex)
Detrusor: smooth muscle; relaxes in filling (sympathetic), contracts in micturition (parasympathetic)

questions.q: Which fibers stimulate contraction of the detrusor muscle?
choices: Somatic S2-S4 via the pudendal nerve
Visceral afferents T11-L2 via renal plexus
questions.explain: Parasympathetic fibers from S2-S4, carried by the pelvic splanchnic nerves, stimulate detrusor contraction and urine expulsion.

questions.q: What effect does sympathetic stimulation have on the detrusor?
questions.explain: Sympathetic fibers (L1-L2) relax the bladder muscle, promoting urine retention and storage.

items.why: Bladder lies posterior to the pubic symphysis in both sexes

questions.q: In both sexes, the urinary bladder lies immediately posterior to which structure?
questions.explain: The bladder lies posterior to the pubic symphysis in both sexes.

items.why: Rectum: posterior to the bladder in males

questions.q: In males, which structure borders the bladder posteriorly?
questions.explain: In males the bladder is bordered posteriorly by the rectum and supported inferiorly by the levator ani and prostate.

items.why: Levator ani: sling pubis->coccyx; supports bladder inferiorly

questions.q: The levator ani muscles form a sling between which bones?
questions.explain: The levator ani muscles are a muscular sling from the pubic bone to the coccyx that supports the bladder inferiorly.

items.why: Prostate: inferior support of bladder; BPH compresses prostatic urethra; DRE

questions.q: A 65-year-old man has urinary hesitancy and a smooth, symmetrically enlarged prostate on rectal exam. Which urethral segment is compressed?
questions.explain: BPH is age-related prostate enlargement that compresses the prostatic urethra, causing hesitancy and incomplete emptying.

questions.q: Why can prostate size be assessed by digital rectal exam?
choices: Its anterior surface abuts the symphysis
Its base projects into the bladder neck
It is enclosed within the levator ani
Its posterior surface lies against the rectum
questions.explain: Because the posterior surface of the prostate lies directly anterior to the rectum, DRE can assess its size, contour, and consistency.

items.why: Uterus: posterior to the bladder in females (bladder-uterus-rectum)

questions.q: From anterior to posterior, which order is correct in the female pelvis?
questions.explain: In the female pelvis the anterior-to-posterior order is bladder, uterus, rectum.

items.why: Vaginal canal: posterior bladder border in females; urethra-vagina-anus

questions.q: From anterior to posterior, which order of openings is correct in the female perineum?
questions.explain: Inferiorly, the female anterior-to-posterior order is urethra, vaginal canal, anus.

items.why: Anus: most posterior of urethra-vagina-anus
Urethra: female ~4 cm (UTI risk); male 18-20 cm, urine + semen

questions.q: Why are females more prone to urinary tract infections than males?
choices: Short urethra lying near the rectum
Long urethra lying near the vagina
Wider ureteric orifices in the bladder
questions.explain: The shorter female urethra lets bacteria reach the bladder more easily, and it lies closer to the bacteria-carrying rectum.

questions.q: Approximately how long is the female urethra?
questions.explain: The female urethra is about 1.5 inches (4 cm) long, below the clitoris and above the vaginal opening.

questions.q: Approximately how long is the male urethra?
questions.explain: The male urethra is about 7-8 inches (18-20 cm) long and carries both urine and semen.

items.why: Internal urethral sphincter: smooth, involuntary; sympathetic contraction prevents semen reflux

questions.q: Which best describes the internal urethral sphincter?
questions.explain: The internal urethral sphincter, at the bladder-urethra junction, is smooth muscle under involuntary control.

questions.q: In males, sympathetic contraction of this sphincter during ejaculation prevents what?
questions.explain: Sympathetic innervation contracts the internal urethral sphincter, which in males prevents reflux of semen into the bladder during ejaculation.

items.why: External urethral sphincter: skeletal, voluntary; pudendal n.; surrounds membranous urethra

questions.q: The external urethral sphincter surrounds which segment of the male urethra?
questions.explain: The membranous urethra passes through the perineal membrane and is surrounded by the external urethral sphincter.

items.why: Prostatic urethra: passes through prostate; compressed in BPH
Membranous urethra: through perineal membrane; fixed, narrow; catheter rupture

questions.q: Forceful urethral catheterization is most likely to rupture which segment?
questions.explain: The membranous urethra is fixed and narrow as it passes through the perineal membrane, so forceful catheterization can rupture it.

questions.q: The membranous urethra passes through which structure?
questions.explain: The membranous urethra passes through the perineal membrane, surrounded by the external urethral sphincter.

items.why: Spongy urethra: runs the length of the penis
External urethral orifice: terminal opening in both sexes
Abdominal aorta gives the renal and gonadal arteries

questions.q: A renal carcinoma invades the left renal artery. That artery is a direct branch of which vessel?
questions.explain: Both renal arteries branch directly from the abdominal aorta.

items.why: Renal arteries: from aorta; kidneys get ~25% of cardiac output

questions.q: About what fraction of cardiac output do the kidneys receive?
questions.explain: The kidneys are among the most well-perfused organs, receiving about 25% of cardiac output.

items.why: Segmental -> interlobar -> arcuate -> interlobular -> glomerulus

questions.q: Segmental renal arteries give rise to which arteries next?
questions.explain: The renal artery splits into segmental arteries, which give off interlobar arteries, then arcuate and interlobular arteries.

questions.q: Arcuate arteries continue as which vessels?
questions.explain: Interlobar arteries lead to arcuate arteries, which turn into interlobular arteries before the glomerulus.

items.why: Renal veins: left is longer, crosses aorta under SMA; receives left gonadal v.; nutcracker

questions.q: Why is the left renal vein usually longer than the right?
choices: The left kidney sits lower than the right
It crosses the aorta to reach the IVC
It drains into the left common iliac vein
It must loop around the left ureter
questions.explain: The left renal vein is longer because it must cross over the aorta to reach the inferior vena cava.

questions.q: Nutcracker syndrome is compression of the left renal vein between which two vessels?
questions.explain: In nutcracker syndrome the left renal vein is compressed between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta.

items.why: IVC: receives renal veins and right gonadal vein

questions.q: The right gonadal vein drains directly into which vessel?
questions.explain: The right gonadal vein drains directly into the lower-pressure IVC, whereas the left drains into the left renal vein.

items.why: SMA: left renal vein passes beneath it (nutcracker)

questions.q: Which vessel passes beneath the superior mesenteric artery, between it and the aorta?
questions.explain: The left renal vein passes underneath the SMA as it crosses the aorta, where it can be compressed (nutcracker syndrome).

items.why: Gonadal veins: left -> left renal v. (left varicocele, pelvic congestion); right -> IVC

questions.q: Where does the left gonadal vein drain?
questions.explain: The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, which can be compressed by outside structures.

questions.q: A man with nutcracker syndrome develops a varicocele. On which side is it most likely?
questions.explain: Left renal vein obstruction raises pressure in the left gonadal vein that drains into it, commonly causing a left-sided varicocele.

items.why: Gonadal arteries: from aorta; testicular via inguinal canal, ovarian in suspensory ligament

questions.q: The gonadal arteries typically arise from which vessel?
questions.explain: The gonadal arteries typically arise directly from the abdominal aorta and descend retroperitoneally.

questions.q: In females, the ovarian artery reaches the ovary within which structure?
questions.explain: Ovarian arteries travel within the suspensory ligament of the ovary.

items.why: Common iliac aa.: ureter crosses them at the brim (stone site); bifurcate into int/ext iliac

questions.q: A kidney stone lodges where the ureter crosses into the pelvis. Which vessels does the ureter cross there?
questions.explain: The ureters cross the common iliac arteries and veins to enter the pelvis, a common site for stones to get stuck.

questions.q: Lymph from the middle third of the ureter drains to which nodes?
questions.explain: Middle-third ureteral lymph drains to common iliac nodes; the lower third drains to common, internal, and external iliac nodes.

items.why: Common iliac veins: formed by int+ext iliac; unite to form IVC

questions.q: The two common iliac veins unite to form which vessel?
questions.explain: The internal and external iliac veins form the common iliac veins, which join to create the inferior vena cava.

items.why: Internal iliac aa.: supply pelvic organs; give umbilical -> superior vesical

questions.q: What do the internal iliac arteries mainly supply?
questions.explain: The common iliac arteries bifurcate into internal iliac arteries supplying pelvic organs and external iliac arteries supplying the lower limbs.

items.why: Internal iliac vv.: receive superior and inferior vesical veins

questions.q: The superior and inferior vesical veins are tributaries of which veins?
questions.explain: The superior and inferior vesical veins drain into the internal iliac veins.

items.why: External iliac aa.: supply the lower limbs

questions.q: What does the external iliac artery primarily supply?
questions.explain: External iliac arteries supply the lower limbs, while internal iliac arteries supply pelvic organs.

items.why: External iliac vv.: join internal iliac vv. to form common iliac vv.
Superior vesical aa.: from umbilical aa. (internal iliac); supply upper bladder

questions.q: The superior vesical arteries are branches of which arteries?
questions.explain: The superior vesical arteries branch from the umbilical arteries, which come from the internal iliac arteries.

questions.q: Which part of the bladder do the superior vesical arteries supply?
questions.explain: The upper bladder is supplied by the superior vesical artery; the lower bladder by the inferior vesical artery.

items.why: Sympathetics: kidney T10-L1 via aorticorenal ganglion; ureter pain T11-L5; bladder L1-L2

questions.q: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons to the kidney originate from which spinal levels?
questions.explain: Kidney sympathetic preganglionics arise from T10-L1 and synapse in the aorticorenal ganglion; postganglionics follow the renal artery.

questions.q: Ureteric pain afferents follow sympathetic fibers back to which cord segments?
questions.explain: Visceral afferent pain fibers from the ureters follow sympathetic fibers retrograde to cord segments T11-L5.

questions.q: Sympathetic fibers to the urinary bladder come from which cord levels?
questions.explain: The bladder receives sympathetic fibers from L1-L2 and parasympathetic fibers from S2-S4.

items.why: Pudendal n.: somatic motor to external urethral sphincter; voluntary control

questions.q: A 72-year-old man leaks urine when he coughs. Damage to which nerve is most likely?
questions.explain: The somatic pudendal nerve supplies the external urethral sphincter, which gives voluntary control of urination.

questions.q: What type of innervation does the pudendal nerve provide to the external urethral sphincter?
questions.explain: The somatic pudendal nerve supplies motor innervation to the external urethral sphincter, allowing voluntary control.
